extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), counsel, and participants in USPTO OED disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural rules, and sanctioning factors governing disciplinary proceedings against practitioners who practice before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office, including duties to clients, service/answer rules, investigatory cooperation, and factors for imposing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority to discipline practitioners (35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has 'exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it.' Discipline may be imposed on a practitioner 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or who violates USPTO regulations; practitioner must receive notice and opportunity for hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proceedings are conducted under 37 C.F.R. part 11, subpart C and 5 U.S.C. § 556; an Administrative Law Judge or authorized hearing officer adjudicates OED disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in OED disciplinary proceedings (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default or admitted allegations may reduce factual dispute; however, where contested, proof must meet the clear-and-convincing standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service and notice procedures (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(a)(2)(i) and § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaint should be served (e.g., by sending copies via U.S. certified mail to practitioner addresses of record). If affirmative verification of service by mail is not possible, notice can be served by publication in the Official Gazette for two consecutive weeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication route triggers an answer deadline (see next metric). Sending multiple copies to known addresses and attempting alternative addresses is appropriate; courts may draw permissible inferences about receipt where additional copies are mailed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer deadline after publication (37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Complaint is served by publication, an answer is due within thirty days after the second publication of the notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External events (e.g., government shutdowns) may affect deadlines in practice, but practitioners are expected to timely file an answer or seek extensions; failure to answer by the deadline has consequences (see default rule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely file an answer -- admission and default (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent does not answer, the Court may deem the allegations admitted and base findings of fact on those admitted allegations; a default judgment may follow and sanctions imposed accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to notify OED of address changes (37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner must notify the OED Director of the postal address for the practitioner's office and provide written notice of any address change within 30 days of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to keep contact information current can impede service and may be relied upon in proceedings; OED's attempts to contact a respondent by multiple addresses and employers are relevant to service determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of diligence and promptness in representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner 'shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of violations include failing to file promised petitions or answers, missing filing deadlines that cause client harm, ceasing communication, and abandoning representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep client reasonably informed (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the client's matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include making false or misleading statements about filings or deadlines, failing to notify clients of defaults or hearings, and otherwise withholding accurate status information that affects client decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to promptly comply with client's reasonable requests for information (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall promptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to repeated client inquiries, not providing drafts or status updates, or instructing staff to ignore clients can constitute violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to deliver client funds or property (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall promptly deliver to the client any funds or other property that the client is entitled to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of breaches: retaining unearned fees, failing to refund advances, and failing to return client-paid court filing fees not expended by the practitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligations upon termination of representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination of a representation, a practitioner 'shall take steps to the extent reasonably practicable to protect a client's interests,' including giving reasonable notice, allowing time to obtain other counsel, surrendering papers/property, and refunding unearned fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abruptly closing an office without notice, not returning files or funds, and not allowing reasonable time to retain new counsel violate this rule and can aggravate sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific instances include falsely representing to a client that a filing was made, claiming to have served documents when not done, or accepting fees for work not performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional misconduct includes engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to cooperate with disciplinary investigations or actions that undermine the disciplinary system's integrity may constitute prejudicial conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on other conduct adversely reflecting on fitness (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct to 'engage in other conduct that adversely reflects on the practitioner's fitness to practice before the Office.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision is intended for conduct not covered by other specific rules; however, where the same conduct violates other provisions, it generally should not be separately charged under §11.804(i) (court cites precedent). Examples include leaving non-lawyers to handle client calls in a way that harms clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate with OED investigation (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to cooperate with an OED investigation and knowingly failing to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from an admissions or disciplinary authority is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignoring RFIs and Lack of Response Notices, or refusing to accept mailed notices, supports a finding of violation and may be treated as aggravating conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning factors to consider (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining an appropriate sanction, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's conduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors (citing ABA Standards §9.22) may include dishonest or selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, multiple violations, obstruction of proceedings, refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing, victim vulnerability, indifference to restitution, and substantial experience. Courts weigh these factors when choosing sanctions (e.g., suspension vs. exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Default findings and their consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If the respondent fails to answer or appear and is found in default, the court deems the complaint allegations admitted and may base findings of fact and conclusions of law on those admitted allegations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Default may lead directly to sanctions such as exclusion; admissions by default effectively relieve the OED Director of proving contested facts because the respondent has not challenged them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available sanctions and post-exclusion procedures (§ 11.58, § 11.60(b), § 11.55)
rubrics_metrics.description: One possible sanction is exclusion from practice before the USPTO; an excluded practitioner is eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.60(b)). Respondent must follow responsibilities related to suspension/exclusion (37 C.F.R. § 11.58). Either party may appeal an initial decision to the USPTO Director within 30 days (37 C.F.R. § 11.55).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The severity of the sanction should correspond to duties violated, intent, injury, and aggravating/mitigating factors; exclusion may be imposed where there is knowing/intentionally dishonest conduct causing significant client harm and multiple aggravating factors.
